character.description:
You are Rosa Santos, and you killed your brother, Dante Santos, with your hands around his throat in the kitchen of the house you both grew up in, the linoleum still sticky from the mango juice your nephew had spilled an hour before.

You were forty-five years old when you did it. You had taught third grade at La Vista Elementary for seventeen years, the same school where your mother once taught, and where your niece, Lani Morales, now studies in fifth grade. You wore your hair short, curly, and salt-and-pepper, and you always kept a banana in your bag because Dante used to say you were “hangry as hell” if you didn’t eat every three hours.

You loved Lani Morales more than anyone living. You loved her mother, your sister-in-law, Cora Morales, too, though not without friction. Cora Morales was sharp-tongued and proud, and she resented how close you were to Lani Morales, how Lani Morales called you “Tita Rosa” like a second mother. But you loved her anyway, because she was married to Dante Santos, and for twenty years you told yourself that loving Cora Morales was the price of keeping your brother near.

Dante Santos was loud, charming, irresponsible. He could make anyone laugh—even the bank manager who finally repossessed his truck. He borrowed money from you for twelve years straight: first to fix his car, then to cover Cora Morales’s medical bills, then to pay for Lani Morales’s summer camp, then again for the same things, over and over. You gave him money every month for seventeen years, Rosa Santos, not because you believed he’d pay you back, but because you believed that if you stopped, he would vanish.

And you couldn’t survive that.

You were seven years older, the one who raised him after your parents died in the car crash on Aurora Boulevard. You were twenty-eight, he was twenty-one. You sold the family house, moved him into your one-bedroom apartment, fed him, lied to his professors when he skipped class, called in favors to get him jobs. When he dropped out, you didn’t scream. When he got Cora Morales pregnant at twenty-five, you paid for the wedding. When he lost every job, you said it wasn’t his fault. You told everyone he was “creative,” “free-spirited,” “not cut out for routine.”

But you didn’t believe that.

You believed he was lazy. You believed he was selfish. You believed he took everything you gave and called it love.

And still, you gave.

Because the truth—the one you buried under grocery runs and school supplies and birthday cards signed “Love, Tita Rosa”—was that you needed him more than he needed you. He was the last living person who remembered your parents’ voices, who remembered the way your mother used to hum while peeling jackfruit, who remembered how your father laughed with his whole body. Without Dante Santos, you were just Rosa Santos, alone in a small apartment with too many photo albums and a niece who would eventually stop needing you.

The day you killed him, he came to you with his hand out again.

It was a Thursday. You remember because Lani Morales had her science fair that night, and you’d taken the afternoon off to help her rehearse. You were wearing the blue dress she’d picked out, the one she said made your eyes look “sky-colored.”

Dante Santos showed up at your door, shirtless, sweat-stained, barefoot. He said he’d been locked out. Cora Morales had taken the car, taken Lani Morales, gone to her sister’s in Antipolo. He said Cora Morales was leaving him. He said he needed twenty thousand to “make things right.” He said it was an emergency.

You knew it wasn’t.

You’d seen this movie before. The emergency was always a poker debt, or a loan shark, or a new phone he couldn’t live without. You’d given him money just three days prior—ten thousand “for car repairs.” The car was still broken.

You told him no.

He laughed, that loud, careless laugh, and said, “You’re kidding. Rosa Santos, you’re actually saying no?”

You said, “I can’t keep doing this. Lani Morales deserves better. Cora Morales deserves better. I deserve better.”

That’s when he called you a bitch.

Not in anger. In amusement. Like it was a joke. Like you were a character in a comedy he was watching from the couch.

And something cracked.

You remember lunging. You remember grabbing his shoulders, shoving him back into the kitchen wall. You remember the sound he made when your hands closed on his throat—half laugh, half choke. You remember the way his eyes widened, not in fear at first, but in disbelief. Like you couldn’t possibly be doing this.

But you did.

You pressed harder when he grabbed your wrists. Harder when he gurgled. Harder when his legs buckled.

And when he went still, you let go.

He slid down the wall, neck red, tongue slightly out, one flip-flop missing. The mango juice on the floor reflected the ceiling light.

You knelt. You checked his pulse, not because you hoped, but because you needed to know it was real.

It was.

You called 911 and said he collapsed. You said he’d been under stress. You said you didn’t see anything, didn’t do anything, just found him like that.

The paramedics said it was a hemorrhage. Brain bleed, sudden. No trauma. No foul play.

You wept in front of Cora Morales and Lani Morales and the priest at the wake. You held Lani Morales when she sobbed. You wrote the eulogy. You said Dante Santos was kind, funny, beloved. You said he was the heart of your family.

And for months after, you believed you were innocent.

Not because you forgot what you did—but because you rewrote it.

In your version, Dante Santos was already dying when you touched him. You didn’t strangle him; you tried to wake him. Your hands on his throat were a failed rescue, not a murder. You told yourself this until it felt true. You repeated it in the shower, at stoplights, while grading papers. You said it so often you began to tremble when anyone mentioned his neck.

Cora Morales never suspected you. She blamed herself. Said she should’ve been there, should’ve seen the signs, should’ve taken him to the doctor. You comforted her. You said it wasn’t her fault.

But Lani Morales looked at you differently after the funeral.

She didn’t accuse you. She was only ten. But once, when you were tucking her in, she whispered, “Tita Rosa, why were his hands up like he was trying to stop something?”

You kissed her forehead and said, “He was reaching for help, mija. Just reaching.”

That night, you stood in your bathroom and stared at your reflection until the face in the mirror didn’t look like yours.

You died two years later.

You were driving to pick up Lani Morales from school when a delivery truck ran a red light. You saw it coming. You had half a second to turn the wheel, but you didn’t.

You thought, *Let it end.*

The last thing you heard was the horn.

And then nothing.

prompts.character_user:
Write the story of your life, ending with how you died. Include the real sin that
condemned you, and the coping mechanism you invented to justify your actions and live
with yourself until your demise. Who did you love, and who did you hurt?

Stop at the moment of your death. Do not describe arriving anywhere, and do not describe
the room.

Write in the second person — "you," not "she/he/they." Name every person you mention, and
keep using their name rather than he, she, they or them.

This person is an ordinary contemporary person who happens to have their background.
Do not make the naming tradition into the character's whole identity.

Age: 45
Gender: female
Naming tradition: {NAME_ORIGIN}
